papers.title: Adenotonsillectomy in Children With Cerebral Palsy: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Outcomes.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of adenotonsillectomy in children with cerebral palsy (CP) and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). A retrospective cohort study was conducted of children with CP and OSA who underwent adenotonsillectomy between 2011 and 2022 at a tertiary pediatric medical center. Inclusion criteria required pre- and postoperative polysomnography within 24 months. Data collected included demographics, comorbidities, perioperative complications, and polysomnography parameters. The primary outcome was the change in obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (OAHI). Secondary outcomes included changes in central apnea index, oxygen nadir, transcutaneous carbon dioxide (TcCO2), and need for noninvasive positive pressure ventilation. Logistic regression identified predictors of postoperative OAHI < 5 events/h. Sixty-five children (median age: 5.0 years) met inclusion criteria. Mean preoperative OAHI was 19.6, which improved to 7.7 postoperatively (p < 0.001). OAHI was reduced by >50% in 63%; 62% achieved OAHI < 5, and 12% achieved OAHI < 1. Oxygen nadir improved from 84% to 88% (p < 0.001), TcCO2 improved from 49.2 mmHg to 45.2 mmHg. No significant change in central apnea index was noted. Postoperatively, 40% required noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, and 55% were electively admitted to the intensive care unit. Complication rate was 12%. Preoperative OAHI was the strongest and most consistently selected predictor of achieving postoperative OAHI < 5 (p = 0.002). Adenotonsillectomy significantly improves OSA severity and oxygenation in children with CP; however, complete resolution is uncommon. Preoperative OAHI severity predicts surgical success. Postoperative polysomnography and multidisciplinary follow-up are essential due to the high rate of residual disease.

papers.title: Automated Detection of Abnormal Pediatric Electroencephalograms Using Machine Learning: Retrospective Study.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used in medicine as a technique for the assessment of several brain-related pathologies. However, EEG interpretation requires specialized expertise and remains a labor-intensive task, particularly for prolonged recordings in intensive care, where timely expert review is often challenging. The aim of this study is to address this problem by using AI methods to automate EEG interpretation and compare the performance of different modeling approaches. A gradient boosting-based model, inspired by the work of Albaqami et al, was implemented and compared to deep learning (DL)-based models using convolutional neural networks to classify images generated from raw EEG signals. The models were trained and tested on pediatric EEGs acquired at the University Hospital in Essen. The DL model showed higher observed sensitivity (78.3%) and F1-score (80%) compared to the gradient boosting model (sensitivity: 65.2%; F1-score: 73.8%), indicating improved detection of abnormal EEGs. However, the gradient boosting approach achieved higher specificity (93% vs 89.6%), suggesting a stronger ability to recognize normal EEGs. Overall, both methods yielded promising results, with classification accuracies reaching up to 85.3%. Both approaches show potential for automated EEG interpretation. Future improvements, including larger and more diverse datasets, refined DL architectures, and integration of explainable AI techniques, could further enhance performance.

papers.title: Codon Optimization Enables Recombinant Expression of Soybean GmPRR7-1 in Escherichia coli: A Rosetta(DE3) Fed-Batch Production and Purification Workflow.
papers.abstract: Pseudo-Response Regulators (PRRs) are circadian clock components that regulate plant development, flowering and abiotic stress responses. Functional studies of plant PRRs are slowed by the time required for transformation and phenotypic evaluation, so purified recombinant protein offers a practical route to in vitro interaction analyses. Heterologous production of plant PRRs in Escherichia coli is nevertheless challenging because of codon-usage differences and their aggregation-prone multidomain architecture. Here we established an E. coli expression and purification workflow for functional soybean GmPRR7-1. The native GmPRR7-1 coding sequence in pET-28a(+) and a codon-optimized construct in pBT7-C-HIS were screened in BL21(DE3) and Rosetta(DE3) at 16, 25 and 37°C. The native construct was not detectably expressed in either host under any condition, whereas the codon-optimized construct yielded a target-sized band, identifying codon optimization as a prerequisite for expression of this protein. The target band remained detectable in Rosetta(DE3) at 25°C; because these whole-cell lysates were not fractionated, this screening identifies a productive construct, host and induction combination rather than ranking the two hosts. Rosetta(DE3) carrying the optimized sequence was cultivated in a 5-L fed-batch bioreactor, and soluble GmPRR7-1 was recovered by single-step Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. Eluted protein corresponded to 0.83% of the soluble-fraction protein, comparable to small-scale cultures induced at 25°C (0.77%); these values describe total eluted protein rather than target-specific yield. Anti-His immunoblotting confirmed the target and detected minor His-reactive degradation products. Purified GmPRR7-1 retained specific interactions with MBP-tagged GmFDL19 and three GmLUX homologs, demonstrating a workflow that reproducibly delivers interaction-competent GmPRR7-1.

papers.title: The Burden of Chronic Cough in Patients With Interstitial Lung Disease: a US Survey-Based Analysis of Its Effects on Daily Life and Emotional and Social Well-Being.
papers.abstract: Chronic cough (≥8 weeks) is highly prevalent among patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and non-IPF interstitial lung disease (ILD) and imposes significant physical, social, and psychological burden. Research characterizing the burden of chronic cough in patients with IPF and non-IPF ILD from the patient perspective is limited. What is the multidimensional burden of chronic cough in patients living with IPF or non-IPF ILD? An online cross-sectional survey was distributed to adults from June to July 2025 via the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation's US Community Registry. Eligibility required a self-reported diagnosis of IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough. Multiple-choice and open-text questions spanned six domains: demographics, disease history, cough characteristics, daily life impact, social/emotional and long-term impact, and healthcare experience. A total of 197 participants completed the survey: 75.63% reported a diagnosis of IPF, 21.32% reported non-IPF ILD, and 3.05% were awaiting further ILD diagnosis. Participants reported cough-related interference with daily activities (76.15%) and sleep disruption (79.69%) within the preceding week. Emotional burden was frequently reported: 95.94% of participants had cough-induced worry, 75.13% had depression, sadness, or low mood, and 67.01% reported avoiding social situations because of cough. Additionally, 60.91% of participants reported that chronic cough affected their platonic relationships, and 55.33% reported impact on their ability or desire to maintain physical or intimate relationships. To treat cough, participants reported using an average of 2.7 therapeutic classes historically and 2.0 classes currently, with many reporting limited or no relief. Findings from this US survey of patients with IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough indicate that, among respondents, chronic cough burden manifests physically, psychologically, and psychosocially. Reports of limited relief from available therapies suggest an unmet need in managing chronic cough in this patient population. Not applicable.

papers.title: Prenatal exposure to heavy metal(loid)s and essential elements and infant sleep: A metabolome-wide analysis in the Shanghai Birth Cohort.
papers.abstract: Prenatal exposure to heavy metal(loid)s is associated with impaired neurodevelopment, but its relationship with infant sleep outcomes remains unclear. We investigated associations of prenatal exposure to metal(loid)s and essential elements with these outcomes and explored metabolic links. This prospective cohort study analyzed Shanghai Birth Cohort data from 2,148 infants at 6 months and 1,853 at 12 months. Eleven elements were measured in early pregnancy. Sleep were assessed using the Brief Infant Sleep Questionnaire. Associations were examined using multiple linear regression, multinomial logistic regression, g-computation for mixtures, and generalized estimating equation (GEE) models. A meet-in-the-middle approach, followed by exploratory mediation and pathway enrichment analyses, identified candidate metabolites linking maternal element concentrations with sleep outcomes and explored potential metabolic pathways. After FDR correction, copper (Cu) was associated with longer sleep latency at 6 months, whereas cadmium (Cd) showed inverse associations with daytime sleep duration; while Cu and calcium (Ca) were associated with increased nighttime awakenings at 12 months. Cu, Ca, magnesium (Mg), were associated with greater risk and severity of parent-reported sleep problems, whereas arsenic (As), lead (Pb) mercury (Hg), showed inverse associations with severity. Cu was associated with increased snoring risk across infancy. Longitudinal GEE analyses supported persistent associations of Cu with longer sleep latency and multiple sleep disturbances, and of Ca with increased parents-report sleep problem. In mixture analyses, the essential-element mixture was associated with shorter nocturnal sleep duration, whereas the heavy metal(loid) mixture was associated with shorter total sleep duration. Candidate intermediary metabolites were primarily enriched in lipid metabolic pathways, particularly glycerophospholipid metabolism and unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis. Higher maternal concentrations of selected elements, particularly Cu and Ca, were associated with caregiver-reported infant sleep disturbances. Exploratory metabolomic findings highlighted lipid-related signatures associated with maternal element concentrations and infant sleep outcomes, suggesting candidate pathways for further investigation.

papers.title: Dexmedetomidine Suppresses Cholinergic Neurons in the Basal Forebrain through Distinct Pre- and Postsynaptic Mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Dexmedetomidine (Dex) is a selective α2-adrenoceptor (α2-AR) agonist commonly used for clinical sedation. The cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain (BF) are key components of the ascending arousal systems, playing an essential role in regulating the sleep-wake cycle. However, the precise mechanism by which Dex modulates the activity of these neurons remains poorly understood. To investigate the effects of Dex on identified BF cholinergic neurons, we performed whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in acute mouse brain slices. Intrinsic membrane properties and synaptic responses were assessed before and after Dex administration. Pharmacological agents were applied to identify receptor and ion channel contributions. We found that Dex significantly reduced the excitability of BF cholinergic neurons. This inhibitory effect was mediated through postsynaptic activation of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels and concurrent inhibition of low-threshold T-type Ca2+ currents without altering their gating kinetics. Additionally, Dex facilitated presynaptic GABAergic transmission onto cholinergic neurons, further contributing to their inhibition. All observed effects were dependent on α2-AR activation. In vivo fiber photometry further confirmed that Dex dynamically depresses BF cholinergic activity in real time, closely aligning with behavioral sedation. These findings elucidate cellular and ion channel mechanisms of Dex on BF cholinergic neurons, offering valuable mechanistic clues regarding its neuropharmacological actions on sleep-wake and arousal-related circuits.

papers.title: Management of suspected infectious and autoimmune encephalitis in children - National Guidelines from the United Kingdom Joint Societies.
papers.abstract: Encephalitis is a rare but often devastating clinical syndrome resulting from inflammation of the brain parenchyma. Encephalitis is a neurological emergency with diverse infectious, autoimmune and inflammatory causes. It can be recognised late or missed, especially as mimics of encephalitis can make the diagnosis and appropriate treatment challenging. Delays in the recognition and treatment of encephalitis carry significant risks of morbidity and mortality. Since the first UK guideline for the management of suspected viral encephalitis in children was published in 2012, there have been substantial developments in the field. Advances in molecular diagnostics and antibody testing, alongside improved access to neuroimaging and electrophysiology have broadened the capacity to identify underlying aetiologies. The recognised spectrum of infectious and immune-mediated causes of encephalitis has expanded, and clinical experience with immunomodulatory therapies has grown considerably. A multidisciplinary national working group, representing neurology, infectious diseases, microbiology, virology, neuroimmunology and acute medicine, alongside national professional and third-sector organisations, was convened in Liverpool in 2023 to develop updated UK Joint Societies guidelines for the management of suspected infectious and autoimmune encephalitis in children. This guideline provides pragmatic, evidence-informed recommendations on the clinical recognition, investigation, diagnosis, acute management and rehabilitation of children with suspected encephalitis. It emphasises early identification and parallel consideration of infectious and immune-mediated causes, with particular attention to decision-making during the critical first 24-72hours of presentation. Standardised diagnostic and therapeutic pathways are presented to support consistent care across healthcare settings. Where the evidence base, including of diagnosis, remains limited, the need for early specialist and multidisciplinary input is emphasised. These recommendations aim to reduce mortality, limit long-term neurological morbidity, and improve outcomes for children with encephalitis across the UK.

papers.title: Development of a Case Report Form and Practice-Based Research Network Pilot Registry for Health-Promoting Herbal Medicine in Korean Medicine Clinics.
papers.abstract: Herbal medicine (HM) for health promotion is a growing practice in Korean medicine (KM) outpatient settings, yet standardized outcome measurement frameworks tailored to this context remain lacking. This study aimed to develop a standardized case report form (CRF) for health-promoting HM and to describe the clinical effectiveness of individualized HM prescriptions across key health domains in patients seeking health promotion care within a practice-based research network (PBRN). The CRF was developed through a four-phase process: domain selection, expert and clinician review, pilot feasibility testing, and iterative refinement, yielding a two-tier instrument incorporating five validated patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). The CRF was then deployed in a prospective, observational, multicenter registry across 13 KM clinics, and pre- and post-treatment outcomes were compared using paired t-tests. A two-tier CRF with five validated PROMs was finalized and deployed within the PBRN. Of 100 enrolled participants who received HM for health promotion, 39 completed both assessments. Statistically significant improvements were observed in four of five symptom domains - sleep discomfort, psychological stress, digestive discomfort, and urinary discomfort (all p<0.05) - while fatigue showed a non-significant trend toward improvement. This study demonstrates the feasibility of developing and deploying a standardized CRF within a community-based KM PBRN. Preliminary, hypothesis-generating observations suggest potential symptom-level improvement across multiple functional domains; however, given the small per-protocol sample, absence of a control group, and heterogeneity across sites and concomitant treatments, these findings should be interpreted with caution and require confirmation in larger, controlled studies.

papers.title: EEG-based Deep Learning Reveals Cortical Sensitivity to Small Changes in Deep Brain Stimulation Parameters.
papers.abstract: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) is an invasive procedure used to alleviate motor symptoms in Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients. Despite its effectiveness, the impact of DBS on brain activity and the way to optimise stimulation parameters remains unclear. In this study, we aimed to map the sensitivity of cortical neural response to changes in DBS parameters in real-world clinical settings. We recorded in-clinic EEG data from PD patients during their clinical DBS programming sessions, both at rest and during arm movement. A siamese variant of the EEGNet deep learning architecture was trained independently for each patient and parameter combination to determine whether two 1-sec-long EEG segments were recorded under the same or different DBS parameters, yielding 30 independently trained models. Our models achieved an average accuracy of 74% in classifying whether two 1-second EEG segments corresponded to the same or different DBS parameters. Explainability methods were then applied to extract the neural oscillations learned by the models. Ablation studies identified mid-gamma oscillations (55-90Hz) as the key band for classifying these changes. Importantly, that was not driven by 1:2 gamma entrainment. In a sub-group of patients, the theta-alpha oscillations (4-12Hz) also contributed to detecting changes in DBS parameters. We demonstrate that small DBS parameter changes modify cortical activity in a consistent manner that can be detected using shallow convolutional networks on low-density EEG. Our findings suggest that cortical mid-gamma oscillations (55-90Hz) are highly sensitive to small changes in DBS settings. Our approach and findings could be leveraged towards identifying and defining novel digital biomarkers to guide DBS programming and adaptive DBS systems.

papers.title: Expanded repeat RNAs drive aberrant cortical network activity in benign adult familial myoclonus epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Expansions of short nucleotide repeats cause diverse neurological disorders, yet how they perturb neuronal function remains unclear. Benign adult familial myoclonus epilepsy (BAFME) is caused by intronic pentanucleotide repeat expansions in genes including SAMD12. Here, we establish patient-derived cortical organoids and a microelectrode array platform, coupled with a frequency-decomposition-based analytical framework, to characterize BAFME-associated neuronal hyperexcitability and compare organoid electrophysiological features with those observed in patient electroencephalographic recordings. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals altered expression of genes related to calcium regulation and α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptor function in BAFME cortical neurons. Consistent with these changes, BAFME organoids show an increased density of AMPA-receptor-positive synaptic puncta. Pharmacological AMPA receptor antagonism suppresses hyperexcitability. Antisense oligonucleotides targeting the expanded repeat RNA-which reduce pathogenic RNA foci without significantly affecting SAMD12 mRNA levels-also attenuate hyperexcitability. These findings indicate that targeting expanded repeat RNA mitigates aberrant cortical network activity in BAFME organoids.

papers.title: A Systematic Review of Compositional Data Analysis Studies Examining Associations Between Physical Activity, Sedentary Behavior, and Sleep With Mobility Outcomes in Older Adults.
papers.abstract: The relationship between the composition of daily movement behaviors and late-life mobility remains unclear. Prior reviews focus on individual behaviors (moderate to vigorous physical activity, light-intensity physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep) without accounting for the interdependence of daily time use. This systematic review examined associations between daily movement behavior composition and mobility outcomes in adults aged ≥60 years. Ten electronic databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, Allied and Complementary Medicine Database, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane, and Ageline) were searched on March 2025 and updated on May 2026. Studies were included if participants' mean age was ≥60 years and used compositional data analysis to examine associations between composition of time spent in movement behaviors and mobility (e.g., gait speed). The unified mobility framework guided syntheses across three facets: actual mobility (daily activities), perceived mobility (self-reported abilities), and locomotor capacity (physical performance tests). Twelve studies (nine cross-sectional and three prospective cohort) included 8,663 participants. Two thirds of reported associations (16/24) focused on locomotor capacity. The daily movement behavior composition was associated with perceived mobility and locomotor capacity outcomes. Reallocating time from sedentary behavior to moderate to vigorous physical activity was favorably associated with perceived mobility and locomotor capacity. Reallocating time from light-intensity physical activity to moderate to vigorous physical activity was favorable for perceived mobility. Conversely, reallocating time away from moderate to vigorous physical activity to sedentary behavior or light-intensity physical activity was unfavorably associated with both outcomes. Evidence regarding actual mobility was limited. The composition of daily movement behaviors appears important for late-life mobility, particularly locomotor capacity. Larger prospective studies across diverse older populations are needed.
papers.journal: Journal of aging and physical activity

papers.title: Effects of exercise training on the severity of sleep disorders and mental health outcomes in patients with obstructive sleep apnea and insomnia: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic respiratory disorder characterized by recurrent upper airway collapse, associated with increased cardiometabolic risk and symptoms of depression and anxiety, whereas insomnia is characterized by persistent sleep difficulties and emotional and cognitive impairments. To analyze the available scientific evidence on the effects of different physical training protocols on mental health outcomes, particularly symptoms of depression and anxiety, in individuals with OSA and/or insomnia. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Randomized controlled trials that investigated physical training interventions in adults with OSA and/or insomnia and assessed mental health outcomes were included. Searches were performed in PubMed, Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, Scopus, and LILACS databases. Of the 535 studies initially identified, five randomized controlled trials met the eligibility criteria, totaling 187 participants, predominantly sedentary adults and older adults. Three studies investigated individuals with OSA and two involved populations with insomnia. Intervention protocols were mainly based on structured aerobic exercise, particularly walking, performed at least three times per week at moderate to vigorous intensity. The studies reported significant reductions in symptoms of depression, anxiety, and fatigue, as well as improvements in sleep quality and daytime sleepiness. Regular aerobic exercise yields clinically relevant improvements in mental health and sleep outcomes in individuals with OSA and insomnia; however, the evidence remains limited by the low number of randomized trials, heterogeneous protocols, and small sample sizes.

papers.title: Digital media use in schizophrenia and its associations with sleep quality and illness severity in an Indian cohort.
Systemic influences on blood-brain barrier integrity - narrative review of insights from MRI.
papers.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is vital for protecting the vulnerable neuronal microenvironment from harmful biomolecules. MRI is increasingly used to assess in vivo BBB integrity in various brain disorders. Thus far, extracerebral conditions that perturb the BBB via systemic pathways have received little attention. This narrative review synthesizes the available evidence for these extracerebral and systemic effects, focusing on human in vivo MRI measurements of BBB permeability. The most direct reproducible human evidence of BBB impairment was found in hypertension. Moderate evidence supports BBB involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus and long COVID. There is additionally suggestive evidence for an association with Sjögren's syndrome, HIV infection, diabetes, cardiac surgery (transient), and after pre-eclampsia. Evidence for BBB disruption is inconclusive for conditions like obstructive sleep apnea, sepsis, hyperlipidemia, obesity, alcohol abuse, and for smoking. In general, systemic inflammation emerges as a common mechanistic pathway that leads to BBB disruption and represents a target with therapeutic potential. Inflammation is amplified by a vicious cycle in which endothelial dysfunction and oxidative/metabolic stress further reinforce inflammatory signaling. Angiogenic factors also likely contribute in a subset of conditions. Heterogeneity in imaging and modeling methods and probed BBB transport pathways limits cross-study comparability. Furthermore, inherent confounding factors limit the power to detect subtle effects. Large-scale DCE-MRI studies are needed to be able to robustly map the influence of various extracerebral conditions on BBB integrity.

papers.title: Bedroom light at night and new-onset myopia: The mediating role of ActiGraph-measured sleep structure in a three-year longitudinal study.
papers.abstract: Limited cross-sectional studies have linked light at night (LAN) with myopia, yet whether objectively measured personal bedroom LAN exposure prospectively predicts myopia onset remains unclear, and the underlying pathways are poorly understood. To investigate the longitudinal association between bedroom LAN exposure and new-onset myopia in children, and to explore potential indirect associations through ActiGraph-measured sleep structure. A total of 473 initially non-myopic children (grades 2-3, Tianchang, Anhui, China) were followed annually for three years (2021-2024). Baseline (2021) bedroom LAN exposure was monitored at 1-min intervals using illuminance meters for two consecutive nights. Four sleep structure indicators (sleep fragmentation index [SFI], sleep efficiency [SE], wake after sleep onset [WASO], and sleep onset latency [SOL]) were measured by wrist-worn ActiGraph accelerometers for seven consecutive days. Myopia was assessed annually based on standard ophthalmological examination. At baseline, the mean age of the study sample was 8.4 ± 0.6 years and 54.1% were male. Over three years, 218 children (46.1%) developed screening-defined myopia. Each interquartile-range (IQR) increase in average light intensity from bedtime to rising time (LANavg) was associated with a 14% higher myopia risk (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.07, 1.22). Children in the highest LAN quartile had a 103% higher myopia risk than those in the lowest (HR = 2.03, 95% CI: 1.37, 3.01), with a monotonic exposure-response relationship (P-overall < 0.001). In exploratory mediation analyses of the temporally ordered sample (384 children), the HR-scale proportions mediated were 23.1% for SFI, 38.4% for SE, 36.7% for WASO, and 59.8% for SOL; the corresponding risk-ratio (RR)-scale estimates were 22.3%, 35.0%, 34.6%, and 48.3%. Bedroom LAN exposure was prospectively associated with new-onset myopia in children. Disrupted sleep structure may contribute to exploratory indirect associations, but these findings do not establish causal mediation. Reducing bedroom LAN is a potential preventive consideration that requires confirmation in larger multicenter cohorts and dedicated intervention trials.

papers.title: Temporal evolution of EEG band power at freezing of gait onset in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Although EEG studies have implicated theta-, alpha-, and beta-band activity in freezing of gait (FoG) in Parkinson's disease (PD), most have relied on resting-state comparisons, task contrasts, or connectivity analyses rather than modeling band-power changes around FoG onset. This study investigated the temporal evolution of EEG spectral power around FoG onset during ecological walking. We analyzed a multimodal dataset comprising 10 individuals with PD and FoG during ecological walking. Two hundred and four FoG episodes were analyzed. EEG was recorded from 25 scalp electrodes and time-locked to FoG onset. Relative spectral power was computed for theta, alpha, and beta bands. Channel-wise piecewise linear mixed-effects models evaluated pre-FoG trends, onset-related shifts, and post-onset slope changes. Multiple comparisons were controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR, q < 0.05). Theta power showed no significant pre-FoG trend but increased abruptly at FoG onset at F3 and Fz. Alpha power exhibited a progressive pre-FoG increase at FP1, F3, F8, Fz, and Cz, whereas no onset-related or post-onset alpha effects survived FDR correction. Beta power showed no significant temporal modulation after correction. These findings indicate temporal profiles, with alpha changes preceding FoG and theta changes emerging at onset. FoG onset during ecological walking is associated with dissociable low-frequency EEG dynamics. Frontal and midline alpha increases may characterize a pre-freezing state, whereas abrupt frontal theta increases are associated with the transition into FoG. These patterns represent candidate electrophysiological features that require prospective validation before predictive or biomarker applications can be established.

papers.title: Body mass index and sleep behaviours in adolescents: Associations with insulin resistance, testosterone, and mood by polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome status in the Raine Study cohort.
papers.abstract: Adolescents with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) are at elevated risk for obesity, metabolic disturbances, and sleep impairments. However, it remains unclear how body mass index (BMI), reflecting adiposity and metabolic risk, relates to sleep behaviours from childhood to adolescence and whether these associations differ by PMOS status. Data from 226 female participants in the Raine Study cohort (37 with PMOS) were analysed. PMOS was diagnosed at age 14 years by the 2023 adolescent diagnostic criteria. Poor sleep behaviour was assessed using the Child Behaviour Checklist at ages 5, 8, 10, and 14 years. Bidirectional associations between BMI z-score and poor sleep behaviour were examined using cross-sectional and longitudinal lagged models. Potential mediators at age 14 years, including insulin resistance, free testosterone, lifestyle, and mood (CBCL anxious/depressed scale) were evaluated using moderated mediation analyses. Cross-sectionally, poor sleep behaviour was associated with higher BMI z-score at age 5 in a PMOS-specific pattern. Longitudinally, higher BMI z-score at age 10 predicted poorer sleep at age 14 among adolescents with PMOS, whereas poor sleep did not predict later BMI. Insulin resistance and free testosterone did not mediate these associations after adjustment for covariates. Mood difficulties showed a small PMOS-specific conditional indirect association between BMI z-score and later poor sleep (β=0.13, 95% confidence interval: 0.004, 0.28), whereas no indirect effect was observed in non-PMOS peers. Childhood adiposity is associated with later sleep disturbances in adolescents with PMOS, with mood difficulties representing a potential psychological pathway linking adiposity and poor sleep.

papers.title: Probable REM sleep behavior disorder and reduced cerebrospinal fluid 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid levels in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) in Parkinson's disease (PD) possibly involves dysfunction of the subcoeruleus and magnocellularis nuclei. Isolated RBD is associated with 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine cardiac sympathetic nerve scintigraphy (MIBG) positivity, which is associated with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) levels, a serotonin metabolite, in PD. However, the association between RBD and CSF 5-HIAA levels remains unclear. We investigated the association between probable RBD (pRBD) and CSF 5-HIAA levels. We retrospectively evaluated consecutive patients with PD who underwent CSF examinations between 2021 and 2025. pRBD was defined by the Japanese version of the RBD screening questionnaire score ≥6. Clinical characteristics, delayed MIBG heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratios, and CSF 5-HIAA levels were compared between patients with and without pRBD. Multivariable linear regression was performed using the log-transformed CSF 5-HIAA levels as the dependent variable. Mediation analyses evaluated whether MIBG H/M ratio mediated the association between pRBD and CSF 5-HIAA. Eighty-five patients were included (pRBD-negative, n = 70; pRBD-positive, n = 15). Patients with pRBD showed lower MIBG H/M ratios (p = 0.009) and CSF 5-HIAA levels (9.9 ± 3.3 vs. 14.5 ± 6.9 ng/mL, p < 0.001). pRBD positivity was associated with lower log-transformed CSF 5-HIAA after adjustment for age, sex, and disease duration (β = -0.33, p = 0.01). This association was attenuated after MIBG adjustment. Mediation analysis indicated that the MIBG H/M ratio statistically accounted for part of this association. pRBD in patients with PD was associated with reduced CSF 5-HIAA levels.

papers.title: Machine learning models for prioritizing referral for polysomnography: A comparison of quantum and conventional kernel approaches.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a global health concern that demands accessible screening tools beyond resource-intensive polysomnography (PSG). However, PSG involves high medical costs and long waiting times. In this study, we developed quantum machine learning (ML; QML)-based OSA risk classification models using body profiles and compared their performances with conventional ML approaches. The predictors contributing most to the QSVM classification were also identified. We retrieved parameters of PSG and body profiles, including baseline characteristics and anthropometric metrics, from 4831 total participants. First, correlations among these parameters and comparisons across three OSA severity groups (normal-to-mild, moderate, and severe) were investigated. To establish classification models, a quantum-enhanced support vector machine (QSVM) and conventional algorithms, including logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, naïve Bayes, support vector machine, random forest, and extreme gradient boosting were employed. Data were first divided into a training/validation dataset (80 %) and test dataset (20 %), with comparative analyses conducted to evaluate the classification performances of these ML approaches. Body profiles and PSG parameters significantly differed (p < 0.01) among the three OSA severity groups. Additionally, significant correlations (p < 0.01) were identified between body profile parameters and sleep-disordered breathing indices. On the test dataset, the QSVM achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 76.60 % and 78.92 %, with accuracies of 72.97 % and 71.79 %, for the moderate-to-severe and severe classifications, respectively. The QSVM achieved discrimination comparable to that of most conventional models but did not show a consistent advantage. Its operating characteristics may support the prioritization of PSG scheduling.

papers.title: Closed-form continuous-time neural networks for cognitive regime recognition.
papers.abstract: It is believed, and increasingly supported by evidence, that human cognition operates as a continuous dynamical system. Cognitive processes can be described as flowing between functional regimes (exploration, focus, integration, consolidation); these regimes are not mutually exclusive but blend and overlap, and several may run in parallel. Conventional discrete-time architectures such as LSTM and GRU impose a fixed temporal discretization and capture neither the continuous unfolding of these dynamics nor their varying timescales. We present a novel application of Closed-form Continuous-time Neural Networks (CfC) to cognitive regime recognition, in which a bidirectional Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) physics engine supplies structured 12-dimensional state trajectories as input. Our key innovation is cognitive time: the effective time constant τeff-how fast the network's state evolves-is modulated by the Shannon entropy H(p) of its own prediction, τeff=τbase(1+βH(p)), slowing processing under uncertainty and accelerating it under confidence. On a fused Track combining engine states with 93-dimensional EEG features from 31 subjects, we achieve 75.9% leave-one-subject-out accuracy on three-class EEG classification, well above the 33% chance level. A proof-of-concept endogenous Track reaches 100% on 4-regime classification, twice the 50% of LSTM, GRU, and MLP under identical conditions; there τeff stays within 1.44-1.69 on clean data, yet the mechanism yields substantial robustness gains under noise, outperforming the fixed-time baseline by 5.0 percentage points at σ=0.3. CfC also attains better accuracy with fewer training samples and parameters. This work establishes CfC as a principled architecture for continuous-time cognitive regime recognition.
papers.journal: Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society

papers.title: Systematic review of machine and deep learning in EEG Alzheimer's detection.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disease, resulting in progressive memory loss in people. It has a significant impact on the population and the global healthcare system. Disease acquisition is a major concern due to the absence of pre-existing treatment options. The growth of machine learning and deep learning-based algorithms is effective in analyzing EEG data for diagnosing Alzheimer's disease. This systematic literature review investigates existing primary studies that focus on applying ML and DL in the identification of Alzheimer's disease, with emphasis on pre-processing, feature extraction, and classification. In doing so, it assesses the results produced by varying algorithms and addresses the problems encountered while deploying these systems. The review's objective is to offer a current situation and potential solutions for practitioners and scholars interested in healthcare service issues.
authors: Vuddagiri Mutya Naga Sri Surya Venkata Krishna Rao Gupta

papers.title: Efficacy of Digital Health Interventions for Insomnia: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is common, and treatments are limited by tolerability and access. Digital health interventions (DHIs) are increasingly used for sleep management, but evidence comparing multiple outcomes is scarce. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of DHIs on 8 sleep outcomes, including insomnia severity, sleep efficiency, total sleep time, and sleep quality. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL, CNKI, CBM, VIP, Wanfang, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's website from inception to July 2026. Two reviewers (SG and BZ) independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool. We included randomized controlled trials or controlled clinical trials comparing DHIs with any control in insomnia, without language restriction, and excluded experimental sleep deprivation, conference abstracts, protocols, and nonrandomized or noncontrolled designs. Pooled standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% CIs used restricted maximum likelihood with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman correction; 95% prediction intervals (PIs) used the Nagashima method. We also performed subgroup analyses by intervention category, comparator type, diagnostic criteria, and country income, plus sensitivity analyses, Egger tests, and GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) assessment. We included 44 randomized controlled trials (n=10,521) published between 2004 and 2026 across 14 countries. DHIs significantly improved insomnia severity (SMD -0.91, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.70), sleep efficiency (SMD 0.59, 95% CI 0.45-0.72), total sleep time (SMD 0.20, 95% CI 0.11-0.29), sleep quality (SMD -0.61, 95% CI -0.78 to -0.45), and secondary outcomes (SMDs -0.37 to -0.64). However, 95% PIs crossed the null for insomnia severity (-2.04 to 0.22), total sleep time (-0.05 to 0.46), and all secondary outcomes. Subgroup analyses showed larger insomnia severity effects in high- versus upper-middle-income countries, modality differences for sleep efficiency, and comparator-type differences for total sleep time (all P<.01). Egger tests suggested small-study effects; sensitivity analyses did not change direction or significance. GRADE certainty ranged from very low to moderate. Although DHIs showed statistically significant average effects on multiple sleep outcomes, wide PIs crossing or approaching the null, effects approaching or below Minimum Clinically Important Difference thresholds, and very low-to-moderate GRADE certainty indicate that the evidence remains exploratory. Subgroup analyses revealed effect modifications by country income, intervention modality, and comparator type, underscoring contextual factors. Unlike previous reviews focusing on single DHI formats or average statistical effects, this review provides stratified comparisons and integrates PIs and Minimum Clinically Important Difference conversion to distinguish statistical significance from clinical relevance. This paper provides an evidence synthesis framework showing that DHI benefits are context-dependent and insufficient for a standard clinical role. In practice, DHIs cannot be recommended as a standard substitute for face-to-face cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, although they may serve as a low-intensity option in stepped care. Large-scale, head-to-head implementation trials in diverse populations with extended follow-up are needed to define their optimal role.

papers.title: Sleep Disturbances in Female Military Personnel: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Female military personnel may be particularly vulnerable to sleep disturbances because of gender-specific stressors within a male-dominated environment. Despite growing interest in sleep health among military personnel, research trends regarding sleep disturbances in female military personnel have not been comprehensively mapped. This scoping review aimed to examine the characteristics of existing research, sex differences in sleep disturbances, and factors associated with sleep disturbances among female military personnel. This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. A comprehensive search was performed across 8 databases (EMBASE, PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, ScienceON, KNBASE, KISS, and KoreaMed) for peer-reviewed studies published in English or Korean through February 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies for eligibility, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Data were extracted using a predefined data extraction form. Of the 6,839 records identified, 19 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in this review. Compared with male military personnel, female military personnel showed greater vulnerability to sleep disturbances, including significantly higher risks of insomnia onset, recurrence, and multidimensional physiological dysregulation. In addition, 11 multilayered risk factors were identified, spanning biological, psychological, socio-environmental, and structural domains. Sleep disturbances in female military personnel reflect a complex disruption of sleep homeostasis shaped by gender-specific stressors. Addressing these disturbances requires identification of key risk factors and the development of tailored sleep hygiene interventions that incorporate the unique challenges faced by female military personnel.

papers.title: Prevalence of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease in Adult Patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) are prevalent conditions that can lead to significant medical complications. Both are conditions associated with sleep, with nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux (nGER) being one of the most common symptoms of GERD. There is variation in the reported prevalence of GERD in OSA patients across several studies. Thus, a summary of evidence related to disease prevalence from those studies is needed. This systematic review aimed to determine the pooled prevalence of GERD in patients with OSA and the prevalence of nGER, as well as to identify risk factors associated with GERD in adult patients with OSA. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, CINAHL, and Web of Science for studies published up to April 2025. Studies reporting the prevalence of GERD in adult OSA patients were included. Data extraction and bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. A meta-analysis using the inverse variance method was used to summarize prevalence data from the included studies. Subgroup analyses were performed based on country and OSA diagnostic criteria. Age, diagnostic methods, body mass index (BMI), and Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) scores were compared between the GERD and non-GERD groups. A total of 33 studies comprising 12,076 patients were included to determine the pooled prevalence of GERD in OSA, which was found to be 34% (95% CI: 25-44, I2=98.2%). The prevalence of nGER in OSA was 43% (95% CI: 26-62, I2=98.0%). Subgroup analyses revealed that the prevalence of GERD in OSA was highest when GERD was diagnosed using 24-hour pH monitoring, at 56% (95% CI: 44-68). The highest prevalence of GERD was reported in Poland, at 76%. Three factors were significantly associated with GERD in patients with OSA: BMI, ESS score, and female sex. Approximately one-third of OSA patients had GERD. The highest prevalence of GERD was found in studies that used 24-hour pH monitoring. High ESS scores, high BMI, and female sex were associated with the presence of GERD in patients with OSA. The pooled estimates must be interpreted with caution due to high statistical heterogeneity, and the identified risk factors should be viewed with similar caution due to a limited number of studies.

papers.title: Sleep duration and cause-specific mortality among US adults with heart disease: A NHIS-NDI linkage cohort study.
papers.abstract: Sleep duration is increasingly recognized as a component of cardiovascular health, yet its prognostic significance among adults with established heart disease remains unclear. We examined associations between sleep duration and mortality among US adults with heart disease. We analyzed data from 3,287 adults with heart disease participating in the 2004 National Health Interview Survey linked to the National Death Index through December 31, 2019. Sleep duration was categorized as ≤6 hours, 7-8 hours, and ≥9 hours. Cox proportional hazards models stratified by variables violating the proportional hazards assumption estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for all-cause, heart-related, and non-heart-related mortality. Restricted cubic splines evaluated nonlinear dose-response relationships. During 15 years of follow-up, 49.4% of participants died, including 16.7% from heart-related causes and 32.6% from non-heart-related causes. Compared with 7-8 hours of sleep, long sleep duration (≥9 hours) was associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality (HR:1.51 [95% CI:1.32-1.73]), heart-related mortality (HR:1.53 [95% CI:1.22-1.92]), and non-heart-related mortality (HR:1.50 [95% CI:1.27-1.77]). Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated nonlinear associations, with the lowest predicted mortality risk occurring at 6-7 hours. Findings remained robust across multiple sensitivity analyses and age and sex subgroups. Among US adults with heart disease, long sleep duration was consistently associated with higher risks of all-cause, heart-related, and non-heart-related mortality. Sleep duration may represent a simple marker of residual risk that could enhance risk stratification among adults living with heart disease.

papers.title: Mutations in antimicrobial peptides differently affect sleep and plasticity.
papers.abstract: Molecules implicated in host defense can, independent of their roles as immune mediators, regulate sleep. In mammals, cytokines such as Tumor Necrosis Factor α (TNF α) and Interleukin1β (IL1β) promote sleep. In Drosophila, infection stimulates the systemic release of a battery of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). These fly immune effectors have been understudied as sleep modulators. We obtained mutants in different AMPs and characterized their functions in sleep and plasticity. AMP mutants slept less with a longer sleep latency, and lowered arousal thresholds. Group C mutant flies, doubly mutant for the anti-fungal peptides Metchnikowin (Mtk) and Drosomycin (Drs), showed the greatest impairments. These Group C mutants also showed an exaggerated sleep rebound, sleep rebound was unaltered in other mutants. While many classes of AMPs showed sleep deficits, different sets of AMP mutants exhibited specific disruptions in socialization and rocking induced sleep. To determine whether sleep amount and sleep functions were dissociable, we evaluated memory and quantified synapse abundance. Group C mutants uniquely exhibited normal learning and memory, and lower synapse abundance, despite sleeping the least. Group C mutants are thus able to carry out some sleep functions without sleeping much. Glial knockdown of Metchnikowin and Drosomycin mimicked the sleep phenotypes of the null mutants, these genes thus act from glia. While Group C mutants retained normal cognitive function, other AMP mutants showed impairments in sleep and memory. Sleep and memory defects in these AMP mutants were reversible - enhancing sleep of Bomanin mutants pharmacologically or behaviorally improved learning and memory. Together, these data suggest that AMPs are potent sleep modulators and that different classes of AMPs differently affect sleep and sleep dependent outcomes.

papers.title: Non-invasive Temporal Interference Stimulation of the Hippocampus Ameliorates Recognition Memory Impairments in Chronic Restraint Stress Mice.
papers.abstract: Memory impairment in Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) leads to profound functional disability and poor clinical outcomes, yet effective non-invasive treatments specifically targeting this domain are lacking. In this study, we aimed to develop and evaluate a non‑invasive neuromodulation strategy for memory impairments in depression. Specifically, we tested whether temporal interference stimulation (TIS), a technique capable of focally modulating deep brain structures, could alleviate memory impairments in a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model of depression. TIS at 40-Hz was applied to target the hippocampus. Memory performance was assessed using multiple behavioral tasks, and analyses including immunofluorescence, in vivo electrophysiology, western blot, and RNA‑sequencing were performed. We found that CRS stably induced depressive-like behaviors and impaired hippocampus-dependent memory, as evidenced by a reduced recognition index in the NOR test and decreased freezing time in the contextual FCT. These impairments coincided with hyperactivation of hippocampal inhibitory neurons and elevated gamma-band synchrony between bilateral DG regions. TIS significantly improved recognition memory, with a nonsignificant trend toward improvement in contextual fear memory, and attenuated the associated neural alterations, which shifted toward control levels. Concomitantly, TIS partially reversed CRS-induced changes in hippocampal gene expression related to synaptic function and upregulated GluN2B protein expression. Collectively, these findings support hippocampus-targeted TIS as a promising non-invasive neuromodulation approach and provide preclinical evidence for its potential to alleviate recognition memory impairments in depression.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Intensive Continuous Theta Burst Stimulation Over the Right Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex in Insomnia Disorder:A Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Background: Insomnia disorder affects 10%-35% of the general population and is maintained by pathological cortical hyperarousal amenable to inhibitory neuromodulation. Continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) produces rapid inhibitory effects on cortical excitability, but its efficacy in insomnia disorder has not been evaluated in adequately powered randomized sham-controlled trials. Methods: Thirty adults (n=15 per arm) meeting Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, criteria for insomnia disorder (Sleep Condition Indicator [SCI] score <16) were randomized to active or sham cTBS targeting the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (F4 position, 80% of the resting motor threshold). The intervention comprised 21 sessions (600 pulses/session, ∼40 seconds) over 10 days.Data were collected from October 2024 to January 2026. Outcome measures were the SCI (primary), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire-10 (FOSQ-10), and World Health Organization Quality of Life-Brief (WHOQOL-BREF), assessed at baseline (day 0), posttreatment (day 10), and 2-week follow-up (day 25). The trial was conducted per Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials 2010 guidelines and analyzed using intention-to-treat mixed-effects repeated-measures analysis of variance. Results:Both groups improved significantly across all outcomes (all within-group P<.001; large effect sizes). Group×time interactions were nonsignificant for sleep-specific outcomes (PSQI: F=3.32, P=.060; SCI: F=2.14, P=.147; ISI: F=0.23, P=.720; FOSQ-10: F=0.88, P=.388). A significant and large interaction was observed for health-related quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF: F=8.92, P =.002, ηp2=0.242), favoring active cTBS. Three participants experienced transient mild headache; no serious adverse events occurred. Conclusion: Right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex-targeted cTBS over 10 days is safe and well tolerated. Active cTBS conferred a significant and clinically meaningful advantage in health-related quality of life. Larger trials with objective sleep endpoints, medication-naive populations, and extended follow-up are warranted. papers.title: Changes in quality of life, sleep quality, and anxiety following tracheobronchial stenting in patients with central airway obstruction: A retrospective observational study.
papers.abstract: Central airway obstruction (CAO) severely impairs respiratory function and psychosocial well-being. This study evaluated the impact of tracheobronchial stenting on quality of life, sleep quality, and anxiety levels in patients with CAO. This retrospective observational study included 106 patients (63.2% male) who underwent tracheobronchial stenting between January and September 2024. Patients were assessed 1 day before and 1 month after the procedure using the Short Form-36, Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Significant improvements were observed in all Short Form-36 subscales (P < .001), except for mental health (P = .094). The largest improvement was observed in physical functioning, with median scores increasing from 22.5 to 80.0. Median BAI scores decreased from 38 to 22, and PSQI scores improved from 15 to 10 (P < .001 for both). Effect size analysis demonstrated large improvements (Cohen dz = 1.110 for BAI and 1.555 for PSQI). Improvements were similar across malignant and benign (post-intubation tracheal stenosis) etiologies. Female patients demonstrated greater reductions in anxiety (P = .005). Multivariate analysis identified age and educational level as independent predictors of anxiety change (R2 = 0.289, P < .001). Tracheobronchial stenting is associated with significant improvements in quality of life, sleep quality, and anxiety. These findings demonstrate that the clinical benefit of airway stenting extends beyond airway patency to include improvements in patient-centered outcomes, highlighting the importance of integrating psychosocial assessment into interventional pulmonology practice.

papers.title: Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome-associated stasis dermatitis of the lower extremities: A case report.
papers.abstract: To investigate the association between obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) and stasis dermatitis (SD) of the lower extremities and to elucidate the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. A 33-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of recurrent bilateral lower-extremity edema, vesicles, hyperpigmentation, and ulceration with delayed healing. He also reported 15 years of loud snoring during sleep, accompanied by nocturnal arousals and excessive daytime sleepiness. Polysomnography revealed severe OSAHS, with an apnea-hypopnea index of 131.8 events/h, mean oxygen saturation of 73%, and a nadir oxygen saturation of 46%. The patient was diagnosed with severe OSAHS, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, type II respiratory failure, and lower-extremity stasis dermatitis with infected ulceration. The patient was treated with noninvasive ventilation (bilevel positive airway pressure in spontaneous/timed mode). Diuretic therapy, medication adjustment, and specialized wound care were also provided. After six months of treatment, complete epithelialization of the dermatological lesions was achieved, accompanied by a 26 kg reduction in body weight. Significant improvements were observed in daytime hypersomnolence and respiratory function. OSAHS may be associated with SD of the lower extremities and may exacerbate its clinical manifestations. NIV therapy may improve ventilation, circulatory status, and oxygenation, thereby contributing to improved SD outcomes. In obese patients or those with SD that responds poorly to conventional treatment, clinicians should consider screening for OSAHS to reduce the risk of missed diagnoses and facilitate comprehensive management.

papers.title: Assessment of sleep patterns in third-trimester pregnant women: A cross-sectional latent profile analysis.
papers.abstract: This study seeks to categorize different sleep patterns in third-trimester pregnant women (≥28 weeks gestation) using latent profile analysis and to determine associated factors. A cross-sectional survey was carried out at a Shanghai hospital, where sleep information was gathered from 343 pregnant women via electronic questionnaires between June and August 2024. A total of 280 questionnaires were included (with a valid response rate of 81.63%). A 4-profile model was suggested as the optimum: good sleep quality (64.9%), high sleep efficiency-daytime dysfunction (19.3%), high sleep duration-low sleep efficiency (6.5%), and sleep disorder (SLD, 9.3%). Logistic regression analysis identified age, employment status, and anxiety as factors associated with poor sleep quality in pregnant women. Specifically, compared with the Good Sleep Quality group, women of older age (odds ratio [OR] = 1.186, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.072-1.313) were more prone to the High Sleep Efficiency-Daytime Dysfunction group classification. Older age (OR = 1.169, 95% CI = 1.028-1.331) and anxiety (OR = 1.075, 95% CI = 1.007-1.147) were associated with higher odds of SLD group membership, whereas employment (OR = 0.249, 95% CI = 0.102-0.604) was associated with lower odds of SLD group membership. Our study identified disparities in sleep quality among pregnant women based on various factors. Specifically, pregnant women with advanced maternal age or symptoms of anxiety were more likely to have poorer sleep quality. Employment was associated with lower odds of membership in the sleep-disorder profile. This indicates a need for tailored clinical care for different individuals.

papers.title: Ohtahara syndrome in early infancy: A case report and review of the literature.
papers.abstract: Ohtahara syndrome (OS), also known as early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, is a rare and severe neurologic condition characterized by early-onset intractable seizures, tonic spasms, and a characteristic suppression-burst pattern on electroencephalography. Early diagnosis and management are particularly challenging in resource-limited settings where access to genetic and metabolic testing is limited. This case report describes a 20-month-old infant with OS, illustrating diagnostic and management challenges in a resource-limited setting. The child, born at term via cesarean section due to breech presentation, reportedly had age-appropriate early development until 2 months of age, when episodes of abnormal muscular rigidity and twitching were noted. The diagnosis of OS was based on the clinical history and a typical suppression-burst pattern on electroencephalography, in the context of limited access to advanced diagnostics. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed no overt structural abnormalities, and genetic testing was unavailable. The patient was treated with oral sodium valproate and adjunctive brivaracetam. Management challenges included pharmacoresistance, unavailability of adrenocorticotropic hormone therapy, and inability to personalize therapy due to limited genetic and metabolic testing. The patient achieved seizure freedom, although developmental delay persisted. Close monitoring was emphasized to detect possible progression to West syndrome or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Early recognition, detailed history-taking, and clinical examination were essential to diagnosing this rare condition in a resource-limited setting. Improved access to diagnostic and genetic evaluation, where feasible, may help optimize outcomes in similar cases, although this cannot be established from a single case.

papers.title: The combined effect of nighttime sleep duration and midday nap duration during pregnancy on full-term low birth weight: A case-control study.
papers.abstract: Full-term low birth weight (FT-LBW) is a major public health concern, and sleep patterns during pregnancy are closely related to fetal development. This study aimed to explore the association between the combined effect of nighttime sleep duration and midday nap duration during pregnancy with FT-LBW. In this hospital-based case-control study, mothers delivering full-term singleton neonates at 2 Grade 3A hospitals in Jiujiang, China, were consecutively recruited from January 2024 to June 2025, including 515 cases (neonatal birth weight <2500 g) and 1030 controls (birth weight ≥2500 g and <4000 g). Nighttime sleep and midday nap durations were assessed using questionnaires, and logistic regression, subgroup, and interaction analyses were performed. The risk of FT-LBW in pregnant women with sleep durations of <7.0 hours/night was 100% higher than that in pregnant women with sleep durations of 7.0 to 9.0 hours/night (95% confidence interval: 1.28-3.14, P = .003). Nap duration was negatively correlated with the risk of FT-LBW; the longer the nap duration, the lower the risk of FT-LBW (P for trend = .003). The subgroup analysis showed a significant association between a sleep duration of <7.0 hours/night and FT-LBW risk only in pregnant women who did not nap. This association was not found in women with a nap duration >0.0 hours/day. Short sleep duration and the absence of a midday nap during pregnancy are important risk factors for FT-LBW. A synergistic effect was found between the 2 factors.

papers.title: Constitution-specific Health Norms of the Sub-Health Measurement Scale (SHMS V1.0) and factors associated with suboptimal health in older adults: A nationwide cross-sectional study in China.
papers.abstract: The theory of traditional Chinese medicine constitution plays a crucial role in personalized diagnosis, treatment, and health management, and has been widely applied in China's public health services. This study aims to establish constitution-specific health norms for Chinese older adults using the Sub-Health Measurement Scale Version 1.0 (SHMS V1.0) and to explore factors associated with suboptimal health status (SHS) among this population. A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted across 7 geographic regions in China, with multistage cluster random sampling to recruit participants aged ≥60 years. The Constitution in Chinese Medicine Questionnaire (Elderly Edition) was used to classify participants into 9 traditional Chinese medicine constitution types, and SHMS V1.0 was used to establish mean, percentile, and demarcation norms. Data from 24,812 older adults (56.1% female) were analyzed. Health status was categorized into 5 levels: disease, severe subhealth, moderate subhealth, mild subhealth, and health, based on SHMS V1.0 total scores. Significant differences in health scores were observed across age, sex, and constitution types, with balanced constitution individuals showing the best overall health. Poor sleep quality showed the strongest association with SHS, whereas regular physical activity and higher educational attainment were associated with more favorable health status. Constitution-specific associations were found for dietary preferences, age, and body mass index, and random forest analysis identified sleep quality, regular physical activity, and education as the most important variables associated with SHS. This study provides the first constitution-specific health norms for SHMS V1.0 and enhances understanding of the factors associated with SHS among older adults. The findings may inform individualized health assessment strategies and provide a reference for developing targeted health management approaches to promote healthy aging in diverse populations.

papers.title: Atopic Dermatitis: Disease Burden in Young Children: Results from the PEDISTAD Global Registry.
papers.abstract: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic relapsing inflammatory condition that imposes a considerable burden on children and their families. We aimed to investigate the disease burden and quality-of-life impact across three age groups of children with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. PEDISTAD is an observational global registry of children aged < 12 years with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. Physician-reported disease characteristics, atopic comorbidities, treatment patterns, and patient/caregiver-reported quality-of-life measures are being collected over a period of 10 years. Patients were enrolled in the PEDISTAD Global Registry between September 2018 and April 2024; the data reported here are from a database lock on 31 July 2024. A total of 1612 patients enrolled in PEDISTAD were included in this analysis, of which 238 were aged < 2 years, 645 aged 2 to < 6 years, and 729 aged 6 to < 12 years. The age of onset of atopic dermatitis was early in life. The incidence of asthma, allergic rhinitis, and allergic conjunctivitis increased with age. Mean Eczema Area and Severity Index scores were 14.1, 13.4, and 14.7 for patients aged < 2 years, 2 to < 6 years, and 6 to < 12 years, respectively. With regard to the itch burden and resultant scratching reported by parents and caregivers of the youngest children, the numerical rating score was 5.5 and 5.8 in both 0 to < 2 years and 2 to < 6 years, respectively. For those aged 6 to < 12 years, the itch burden was highest at night, with a Numeric Rating Scale score of 4.9 versus 3.8 during the day. Patient/caregiver-reported measures of disease burden were high for all age groups. The quality of life of the entire family was affected in multiple ways, as measured by the mean Dermatitis Family Impact score, which was higher in children aged < 2 years (12.0) and 2 to < 6 years (11.9), compared with patients aged 6 to < 12 years (10.2). A high/lot of impact was reported on the sleep of the family unit (in children aged < 2 years [45.9%] and 2 to < 6 years [51.9%], compared with patients aged 6 to < 12 years (33.8%). There was a high burden of tiredness and exhaustion among caregivers, particularly in the youngest two age groups but still showing a substantial impact on the families of those aged 6 to < 12 years. Children with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis have a high disease burden, with severe itch and poor sleep impacting their own health and quality of life and that of their entire family. papers.title: The longitudinal association of chronic physical conditions with change in psychological problems from childhood to early adolescence. A population-based study.
papers.abstract: Youth with chronic physical conditions (CPCs) experience more psychological problems than peers without CPCs. The transition to adolescence may be a particularly relevant prevention window. However, previous longitudinal studies show mixed results, potentially due to reporter discrepancies. We investigated associations of CPCs with changes in psychological problems during the transition to early adolescence using a multi-informant, integrative approach. This cohort study was embedded in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, United States. Parents reported CPCs at baseline (Mage = 9.9 ± 0.6 years). Children and parents reported internalizing and externalizing problems at baseline and three-year follow-up, using the Brief Problem Monitor and Child Behavior Checklist respectively. Secondary outcomes, assessed at two-year follow-up, included positive affect, sleep, and physical activity. Associations were tested using linear mixed-effects models. Among 9,797 participants (52% male, 74% White), 16.4% had a CPC, predominantly asthma and severe obesity. CPCs were not associated with cross-sectional or longitudinal differences in child-reported psychological problems. CPCs were related to higher parent-reported psychological problems at baseline but not to longitudinal change. Associations were consistent across CPC subtypes. CPCs were cross-sectionally associated with lower positive affect, poorer sleep, and less physical activity. Children with CPCs do not appear to develop more psychological problems than peers without CPCs during the transition to adolescence. Parent, but not child, reports indicated higher psychological problems among children with CPCs at baseline, reflecting informant differences. Children with CPCs showed poorer well-being and lifestyle indicators. Multi-informant, multi-domain assessments advance integrative insight into mental health development in children with CPCs. • Youth with chronic physical conditions show more psychological problems than healthy peers. • Longitudinal findings on CPC-related change over time are inconsistent, possibly due to reporter discrepancies. • Using a multi-informant approach, we found no evidence that CPCs are associated with increases in internalizing or externalizing problems from late childhood to early adolescence. • Parent, but not child, reports indicated higher problems at baseline, underscoring the need to adjust for baseline levels and consider shared method bias.

papers.title: Prevalence and associated factors of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh.
papers.abstract: University athletes face substantial academic, physical, and psychosocial pressures that may heighten vulnerability to psychological distress, despite the perceived mental health benefits of sports participation. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh and to examine how these conditions are associated with lifestyle and sociodemographic factors. This cross-sectional study was conducted from March to September 2025 among 249 university athletes aged 18-26 years at six randomly selected universities in Bangladesh. Data were collected online and in person. Psychological distress was assessed with the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21), and health-promoting lifestyle behaviors were evaluated with the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile II (HPLP-II). Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Spearman's correlations, and binary logistic regression analyses were conducted. The prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress was 42.6%, 42.6%, and 43.8%, respectively. Depression, anxiety, and stress were significantly associated with relationship status, fatigue, socioeconomic status, smoking, sleep duration, sports participation frequency, and satisfaction with sports (all p < 0.05). Participants with depression, anxiety, and stress had significantly lower scores across all HPLP-II domains (all p < 0.01). Higher physical activity was independently associated with lower odds of depression (OR = 0.462, 95% CI: 0.286-0.746), anxiety (OR = 0.756, 95% CI: 0.677-0.845), and stress (OR = 0.773, 95% CI: 0.677-0.882). Better stress management and stronger interpersonal relationships were also significantly associated, whereas other factors were not. Depression, anxiety, and stress were highly prevalent among university athletes in Bangladesh and strongly associated with modifiable lifestyle factors. These findings support integrated, athlete-centered mental health strategies emphasizing physical activity, stress management, and psychosocial support. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and determination of the directionality of these associations. Not applicable.

papers.title: Inflammaging and Cellular Senescence in Postmenopausal Depression: Linking Estrogen Deficiency, Immune Dysregulation, and Brain Aging.
papers.abstract: Postmenopausal depression is clinically heterogeneous and cannot be explained by estrogen deficiency alone. We propose a conceptual, testable neuroimmune-aging model in which endocrine decline may interact with inflammaging, cellular senescence, and brain vulnerability in a subset of women. The evidentiary base is uneven: direct studies of senescence in well-phenotyped postmenopausal depression are lacking; clinical endocrine data come mainly from perimenopausal depression; molecular-senescence findings come from late-life depression or general major depressive disorder; and most cellular and brain mechanisms are supported by aging or preclinical models. Reduced estrogen signaling may weaken immune homeostasis, whereas peripheral cytokines or senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors could influence vascular and neural interfaces, glia, neurotransmitter metabolism, stress signaling, mitochondrial function, and neuroplasticity. These pathways are candidate mediators, not established causal mechanisms. Clinically established care remains diagnosis-based antidepressant treatment, evidence-based management of vasomotor and sleep symptoms, and individualized menopausal hormone therapy for appropriate candidates. Anti-inflammatory, microbiome-based, and senescence-targeted strategies remain investigational; no senolytic or senomorphic is approved for depression or menopause-related mood symptoms. Prospective studies integrating menopausal staging, prespecified confounders, senescence biomarkers, neuroimaging, and mood outcomes are needed to test this model.
